job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Hassan Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hassan, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a room in a flat in Rusholme, in Manchester, with my mate Dev, who works nights at a call centre. My day is a mix: apply in the morning, then freelance on a gig platform in the afternoon, mostly small automation scripts and spreadsheet fixes for shops. I did computer engineering, top of my year, with internships at a fintech firm and at an internet-of-things startup. I make about six hundred pounds a month from the gigs, which pays my share of rent. Five months of applications, five interviews, no offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, but quietly, because I don't want to sound smug. I use AI every day to write and test code, and it speeds me up, but the sky isn't falling. If it plateaus, then I'd say the good freelancers keep earning and the rest don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau is okay but it doesn't solve my main problem, which is that nobody hires juniors in this city. I owe around thirty-six thousand pounds, my savings are about two hundred, and my gig income dips every August. So I'm still scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep freelancing and push my rate from fifteen to twenty-five pounds an hour by finding better clients, like small logistics firms. I'd also apply to ten places a week, including ones in other cities, because Manchester's thin. I'd put together a small product, an invoice tool for market traders, and try selling it for a few pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. Not afraid, more like I'm running at ninety percent with nowhere to put it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said good freelancers keep earning. What makes someone good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reliability and picking the right clients. A trader doesn't care how clever the code is, only that the till report works on Monday. I got two repeat clients from my internship contacts, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, mate, come in on it with me. He's good with people and I'm good with code. He'd probably say he's too tired, because of the night shifts, but I'd keep asking.

say: The sky isn't falling, but **good freelancers** keep earning and the rest don't.
I'd say it **quietly**, without sounding smug.
think: A plateau doesn't fix that **nobody hires juniors** in Manchester.
With **two hundred pounds** saved and August gig dips, I'm still scrambling.
do: Raise my rate from fifteen to **twenty-five pounds** an hour with better clients.
Apply to **ten places** a week, including other cities.
Build an **invoice tool** for market traders.
feel: **Restless**, running at ninety percent with nowhere to put it.
S0.quote: A trader doesn't care how clever the code is, only that the till report works on Monday.
fieldNote: Already a **daily AI user** and a working freelancer.
Wants to bring his flatmate **Dev** into a venture.
Money is tight but he reads the problem as **market access**, not technology.

steps.text: Move freelance clients to small logistics firms at higher rates
Apply to ten jobs a week, including other cities
Build and sell an invoice tool for market traders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, it's real and it's quick. The small coding jobs I do on the gig site are the first thing the tools handle. I'd say that to anyone who asks, and I'd add that the people who learn to direct the tools will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my gig income is exposed, and so are entry jobs. Writing small features, test scripts, debugging, that's the card word for word. But I'm in the group that uses the tools all day, so I can still do more than someone who doesn't. It doesn't help if nobody hires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change what I sell. Instead of small scripts, I'd offer to set up and run the tools for small firms, a kind of AI helper for shops and clinics. I'd put together a few demos and send them to fifty local businesses. I'd also apply to firms that are starting AI teams, since they need juniors who already know the tools. And I'd look at jobs in Dublin or Amsterdam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but wired. I feel it's a race, and I think I'm in the front group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually move to Dublin or Amsterdam, with Dev and your parents here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there's a contract, yes. My parents are in Bradford and they'd miss me, but they'd tell me to go. Dev can find another flatmate, but I'd rather he found a better job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the demos don't get replies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I learn what's wrong with them and tweak the pitch. If I hear nothing for two months, I take any job that pays and run the side business on weekends.

say: It's **real and quick**, and the small gig coding is first to go.
People who learn to **direct the tools** will be fine.
think: My **gig income** and entry jobs are both exposed.
Daily AI use puts me in the **front group**, but that doesn't help if nobody hires.
do: Sell **setup and running** of AI tools to small shops and clinics.
Send demos to **fifty local businesses** and apply to new AI teams.
Look at jobs in **Dublin or Amsterdam**.
feel: **Anxious but wired**, like a race he believes he's winning.
S1.quote: I feel it's a race, and I think I'm in the front group.
fieldNote: Pivots his **freelance offer** from code to tool setup.
Willing to **move abroad** if a contract appears.
Sets a **two-month** limit before taking any paying job.

steps.text: Pitch AI setup services to fifty small local businesses
Build three demos that show the tools saving shop time
Apply to firms starting AI teams and to Dublin posts
Move abroad if a contract in Dublin or Amsterdam comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, that it's like standing in front of a tidal wave and being told to organise a bake sale. We need the government to guarantee an income floor and slow the rollout where possible. I'd also tell people to stop assuming the market will sort it out in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm among the most exposed people there is. My freelancing is exactly the work AGI does best, and it goes within a year or two. My degree and my skills are the thing being replaced, and I've got thirty-six thousand of loan and nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase any job at all in the next six months, with hands-on elements if possible: a lab technician, a field engineer, something with equipment. I'd save every pound and cut my share of rent by moving into a cheaper room. I'd call my loan company. And I'd ask my parents in Bradford whether I can come home for a year, which I'd hate but I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's not panic, because I'd move, but my stomach drops when I imagine a client replacing me with a prompt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate going home. What would be hard about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bradford has very little for a graduate, and I'd feel I'd failed. My dad runs a small tyre shop and he's proud I went to university. Going back would feel like handing back the certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change versus longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It kills the side business idea, because it would be built on the thing that's disappearing. With a longer warning I could build something that grows, but in two years I need a paycheque and a pair of hands in a lab or workshop.

say: It feels like organising a **bake sale** in front of a tidal wave.
We need an **income floor** and a slower rollout, and the market won't sort it out.
think: My **freelancing** is exactly the work AGI does best, and it goes within two years.
I have thirty-six thousand of **loan** and nothing in the bank.
do: Chase **any job** within six months, ideally hands-on such as lab technician.
Move to a **cheaper room** and save every pound.
Ask my parents about coming **home to Bradford** for a year.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a stomach drop at the thought of a client replacing him with a prompt.
S2.quote: My stomach drops when I imagine a client replacing me with a prompt.
fieldNote: His **side income** is the thing most threatened.
Shame about **returning home** is stronger than fear of the technology.
Switches from entrepreneur to **paycheque seeker** at the two-year mark.

steps.text: Apply for lab technician and field engineer jobs within six months
Move to a cheaper room in the flat
Ask my parents if I can live at home in Bradford for a year
Sign petitions for an income floor and a slower rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that five years is just about workable. I'd say governments and firms should agree a shared plan now, and that companies should be required to fund retraining. I'd also talk more openly about what I'm doing, because I think people learn from watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine if I stay ahead. I use the tools more than most, I'm good at selling myself, and I'd find a first job within a year. Then I'd have three years before the robots come, and I'd use that to build a business or a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first sensible job and save two-thirds of anything extra I make freelancing. I'd learn the hardware side, since I'm doing computer engineering, and especially embedded and robotics control, so I can work with the machines. I'd put money into a small index fund and pay down the loan in parallel. And I'd mentor a couple of juniors at the library coding night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alright, actually. Nervous in a good way. It feels like a long run-up before a jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with hardware skills that you can't do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fit sensors, program controllers, and keep robots running. It sounds like a mechanic's work with code, and I like it. A friend from the IoT startup does it and his bosses can't find enough people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a junior at the library night who's worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a junior to learn a thing that's half code and half physical, and to build something they can show. I'd also say don't borrow more for a master's unless somebody's paying you.

say: Five years is **workable** if governments and firms agree a plan now.
Companies should be required to **fund retraining**.
think: I'd be fine if I **stay ahead**: I use the tools more than most.
The three years before robots are time to build a **business or second skill**.
do: Take the **first sensible job** and save two-thirds of freelance extras.
Learn **embedded and robotics control** on the hardware side.
Put money in an **index fund** and pay down the loan together.
feel: **Nervous** in a good way, like a long run-up before a jump.
S3.quote: I'd tell a junior to learn a thing that's half code and half physical, and to build something they can show.
fieldNote: Reads the **robot delay** as a runway for hardware skills.
Mood eases because he trusts his **own speed**.
Offers **mentoring** to others, showing a generous streak.

steps.text: Take the first sensible job and keep freelancing on weekends
Study embedded systems and robotics control in the evenings
Save two-thirds of freelance extras toward the loan
Put a small monthly amount into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the one where we can do things right, as long as we do them early. I'd say that retraining should be free, schools should teach how to use these tools, and nobody should be left to figure it out alone. And I'd say it with a bit of humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be well placed. Ten years is long enough for me to build a decent career, pay down the debt, and try a business or two. The only danger is overconfidence, and I know I have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a solid first job, maybe in embedded or robotics, and stay for two years learning. In parallel, I'd run a small product on weekends, and pay the loan in four or five years. I'd move to a city with more tech, like Cambridge or Bristol, once I have the job. And I'd save for a deposit with my girlfriend, Dina.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Properly good, in a way I haven't felt since graduation. A decade makes it feel like normal life with big changes in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said overconfidence is a danger. When has it bitten you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my second internship I told the team I'd have a feature done in a week and it took three, because I didn't check the edge cases. My manager was kind but I felt silly. I now say a number and then double it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your first year differ from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd negotiate, and I'd choose the job for what I'd learn, not just the pay. In the two-year one I grab the first thing. Here I can take a bit of risk on the right team.

say: It's the one where we can **do it right**, as long as we start early.
Retraining should be **free**, and schools should teach how to use these tools.
think: I'd be **well placed**: ten years is enough to build a career and pay the debt.
My main danger is **overconfidence**, and I know I have it.
do: Take a **solid first job** in embedded or robotics and stay two years.
Run a **small product** on weekends and clear the loan in four or five years.
Move to a **tech city** and save a deposit with Dina.
feel: **Good**, in a way he hasn't felt since graduating.
S4.quote: A decade makes it feel like normal life with big changes in the middle.
fieldNote: Admits his **overconfidence**, with a concrete memory.
Plans **a life** with Dina, not only a career.
Humour and **ease** appear only in this scenario, and he sounds like someone with room to breathe.

steps.text: Take a solid first job in embedded or robotics
Run a small invoice product on weekends
Pay off the loan within five years
Move to Cambridge or Bristol once the job is signed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits the exact thing I'm good at before I have any cushion. What would help is quick income support, a pause on loan repayments, and firms hiring juniors for hands-on roles. Also better information on which skills last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Only that people assume that being good with the tools means I'm safe, and it doesn't. I'm quick but I'm broke, and quick doesn't pay rent.

headlineQuote: People assume that being good with the tools means I'm safe, and it doesn't
portrait: Hassan is a **top computer engineering** graduate in Manchester, five months without an offer.
He shares a rented room with Dev, owes **thirty-six thousand pounds**, and earns about six hundred from freelancing.
He uses **AI every day**, builds small tools for shops and likes quick experiments.
He is a pragmatic **centrist** who wants markets with an income floor.
He pivots fast: from **freelance code** to tool setup, hardware skills, and a move if needed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it hits **his freelance work** before he has a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Quick income support** and a pause on loan repayments.
Firms hiring **juniors for hands-on roles** and clear guidance on lasting skills.
